samasa.literal: those of which elephants and horses are the first
samasa.sense: elephants, horses and other such treasures

morph.note: Neuter plural, though the nouns it gathers are mixed (रत्नानि n., मणयः m.): a relative covering things of different genders is put in the neuter. Its correlative (तानि) is understood with समस्तानि.
Present of the athematic √भा: भा + अन्ति → भान्ति, ‘they shine’.
Taddhita abstract/collective in -ya with vṛddhi (त्रि → त्रै): त्रैलोक्य ‘the triad of worlds’.

mantras.anvaya: प्रभो, त्रैलोक्ये यानि रत्नानि मणयः गजाश्वादीनि वै (सन्ति), (तानि) समस्तानि तु साम्प्रतं ते गृहे भान्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यानि … त्रैलोक्ये) gathers the treasures; the main clause (समस्तानि … भान्ति) says where they are now.
mantras.lit: Whatever jewels, gems, elephants, horses and the like there are in the three worlds, O lord, all of them now shine in your house.
mantras.tr: ‘Lord, every treasure of the three worlds — jewels, gems, elephants, horses and all the rest — now shines in your palace.’

comm.t: The servants begin the catalogue of Śumbha’s plunder (5.93–99). The general statement comes first: every treasure of the three worlds is now in his house.

The list fills out what the chapter’s opening stated briefly: the brothers took over the offices of Indra, the Sun, the Moon, Kubera, Yama, Varuṇa, Vāyu and Agni (5.2–4). Each treasure named below belonged to one of those gods.

Nominative singular of the s-stem उच्चैःश्रवस्: the final -as becomes -āḥ (cf. वेधाः, चन्द्रमाः).

mantras.anvaya: ऐरावतः गजरत्नं पुरन्दरात् समानीतः; अयं पारिजाततरुः च, तथा एव उच्चैःश्रवाः हयः (समानीतः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: One participle (समानीतः) serves three subjects; the copula and its repetition are understood.
mantras.lit: Airāvata, the jewel among elephants, has been brought from Purandara; and this Pārijāta tree, and likewise the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
mantras.tr: ‘Airāvata, finest of elephants, has been taken from Indra; so too this Pārijāta tree, and the horse Uccaiḥśravas.’

comm.t: The first spoils named are Indra’s: his elephant Airāvata, the Pārijāta tree of his heaven, and the horse Uccaiḥśravas.

All three are treasures that came up from the churning of the ocean; the messenger himself says so of the horse (5.110, क्षीरोदमथनोद्भूतम्). Possessing them, Śumbha has taken the visible marks of Indra’s kingship.

sandhi.note: Final m becomes anusvāra before h; before the vowel of एतत् it stays m; एतत् and तिष्ठति are simply written together.
Final t becomes d before a vowel and before v; -aḥ before a becomes -o and the a is elided (वेधसोऽद्भुतम्).

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (भूत ‘being, become’ as final member marks identity)
samasa.alt: भूत at the end of a compound is sometimes taken as ‘like’ (रत्नम् इव); here identity fits better, since it is being counted among the jewels.

morph.note: Imperfect of √अस् with augment and the inserted ī of this root before -t: आस्-ई-त्, ‘was’.
Genitive singular of the s-stem वेधस् ‘the Ordainer’, a name of Brahmā (nom. वेधाः).

mantras.anvaya: यत् वेधसः अद्भुतम् आसीत्, एतत् हंससंयुक्तं रत्नभूतं विमानम् इह आनीतं ते अङ्गणे तिष्ठति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause विमानम् … तिष्ठति with its qualifiers; a relative clause (यत् … आसीत्) identifies the car’s former owner.
mantras.lit: This swan-yoked aerial car, a very jewel, brought here, stands in your courtyard — that which was the wonder of Vedhas.
mantras.tr: ‘In your courtyard stands this swan-drawn chariot of the skies, a true treasure brought here — once the marvel of Brahmā.’

comm.t: Next is Brahmā’s own vehicle: the aerial car drawn by swans, now parked in Śumbha’s courtyard. Even the Creator has been stripped.
The swan (haṃsa) is Brahmā’s mount in Purāṇic iconography; its car here shows that the demons’ conquest reached beyond Indra’s heaven to the Creator himself.

from Kubera; a + ī → e by guṇa (6.1.87)

samasa.literal: (a garland) in which the mud-born (lotuses) are unwithered
samasa.sense: a garland of lotuses that never fade

morph.note: Perfect of √दा: reduplicated द-दौ, with the -au ending that ā-roots take in the third singular.
Possessive taddhita in -in (किञ्जल्क ‘filament of a lotus’ + इनि), feminine -inī: ‘having filaments’, i.e. of fresh, full-blown flowers.

mantras.anvaya: एषः महापद्मः निधिः धनेश्वरात् समानीतः; अब्धिः च किञ्जल्किनीम् अम्लानपङ्कजां मालां ददौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: a participial one (निधिः … समानीतः) and a finite one with ददौ, whose object मालाम् has two qualifiers.
mantras.lit: This treasure, Mahāpadma, has been brought from the lord of wealth; and the Ocean gave a garland full of filaments, of unfading lotuses.
mantras.tr: ‘This treasure, the Mahāpadma, was taken from Kubera; and the Ocean gave you a garland of never-fading lotuses, fresh with their filaments.’
mantras.tr_note: ‘You’ is supplied: the Ocean’s gift is to Śumbha, as the context makes clear.

comm.t: Kubera, lord of wealth, has lost the Mahāpadma, and the Ocean has given a garland of unfading lotuses. The Ocean’s gift is phrased as a gift (ददौ), not a seizure: the conquered gods now pay tribute.
Classical lists of Kubera’s nine treasures (nidhi) include Mahāpadma. Its loss marks the seizure of Kubera’s office, one of those named at the chapter’s opening (कौबेरम्, 5.3).

morph.note: Neuter nominative of the -in stem स्राविन् (√स्रु + ṇini, with vṛddhi): the final n is dropped, leaving -स्रावि.
Taddhita in -a with vṛddhi of the first vowel (वरुण → वारुण): ‘of Varuṇa’, cf. कौबेरम्, याम्यम् in 5.3.

mantras.anvaya: ते गेहे वारुणं काञ्चनस्रावि छत्रं तिष्ठति; तथा यः पुरा प्रजापतेः आसीत्, अयं स्यन्दनवरः (ते गेहे तिष्ठति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel statements of place; in the second the verb is understood, and a relative clause names the chariot’s former owner.
mantras.lit: Varuṇa’s parasol, streaming gold, stands in your house; likewise this finest of chariots, which formerly was Prajāpati’s.
mantras.tr: ‘Varuṇa’s parasol, raining gold, stands in your palace, and so does this superb chariot that once belonged to Prajāpati.’

comm.t: Varuṇa’s gold-showering parasol and Prajāpati’s chariot complete the list of royal insignia. The parasol is the classic sign of sovereignty; its owner has lost his rule (वरुणस्य, 5.3).
